title: El Crimen Del Padre Amaro
full_review:
The controversial Mexican melodrama "The Crime of Father Amaro" (Goldwyn) presents a corrosive view of the Catholic Church as an institution and priests in particular. It is necessary to detail the events of the film in order to demonstrate why this is the case.

The movie is based on an 1875 novel by Jose Maria Eca de Queiroz, which director Carlos Carrera has updated to present a cynical vision of the church and its priests.

The movie opens as the idealistic young Father Amaro (Gael Garcia Bernal) arrives in his rural parish. He quickly realizes that his pastor, Father Benito (Sancho Garcia), is having an affair with the cook, Sanjuanera (Angelica Aragon), and that the pastor feels justified in taking money from a notorious local drug lord to fund a hospital.

Yet Father Amaro soon finds himself tempted by the cook's beautiful 16-year-old daughter, Amelia (Ana Claudia Talancon), a catechism teacher who is passionately attracted to the handsome cleric.

When a newspaper expose appears about Father Benito and the drug kingpin's financial relationship, the bishop (Ernesto Gomez Cruz) gets the local mayor to pretend that they generously paid for the hospital construction themselves. The bishop also has the ambitious Father Amaro write this fiction to the paper as an official denial.

Meanwhile in the mountains, Father Natalio (Damian Alcazar) has become a thorn in the bishop's side by practicing liberation theology among the poor and rebels in the area. So the bishop sends his protege Father Amaro to visit the earnest priest with orders to leave his post, but Father Natalio refuses, feeling he is needed by the peasants. The bishop retaliates by excommunicating him and making sure no one else will hire him.

As Father Benito decides he has sinned and breaks off with Sanjuanera, Father Amaro and Amelia begin an impassioned affair. Father Amaro lies to the sacristan that he needs a private room where he can instruct Amelia about entering the convent. Instead, he places the silken robe from the statue of Our Lady of Guadalupe around Amelia and they go to bed. Soon Amelia mistakenly expects he will leave the priesthood and marry her.

When Father Benito learns of the affair, he confronts Father Amaro, whose sly response is tantamount to blackmail: if Father Benito tells on him, so too will Father Amaro rat on Father Benito to the bishop. With Father Benito's silence assured, Father Amaro coldly fires the sacristan who had discovered the couple fornicating.

Angry when Amelia becomes pregnant, Father Amaro suggests an abortion. After her old boyfriend refuses to marry her, the despairing girl is led by Father Amaro to a midnight abortionist, but she bleeds to death after the procedure.

It is believed by the parishioners that Amelia's ex-boyfriend was responsible and that Father Amaro heroically tried to save her life. At the funeral Mass a furious Father Benito leaves Father Amaro's poisonous presence as it is apparent that the now-thoroughly corrupt cleric will continue the lies and hypocrisy to protect his career.

The film's slanted perspective is clear in that the one uncorrupted priest is punished with the most severe punishment -- official excommunication -- by a mendacious bishop whose only interest seems to be in wielding power. The older priest has no trouble rationalizing being part of a drug-money-laundering scheme, although at least he eventually recognizes and rejects his sins of the flesh.

Overall, however, the film piles one egregious priestly hypocrisy on top of another committed by official church figures who will stop at nothing, even the loss of life, to protect their positions. Under the guidance of his pastor and his bishop, the newly ordained Father Amaro goes from a desire to serve the poor to breaking his vow of chastity, rejecting the sacredness of life and ending up as a self-aware and calculating monster. The obvious conclusion is that the church is only concerned about preserving what is seen as an abusive and oppressive level of power over its disposable people.

Blasphemous scenes in which a cynical old woman tosses the Eucharist on the floor for her cat to snatch, and of Amelia playing seductress in the cloth that had been draped on the statue of the Blessed Virgin, should be especially hurtful to Catholics.

The movie's shallow characterizations only underline the film's vicious perspective that leaves one both saddened and outraged by its distortions.

Subtitles.

Due to desecration of the Eucharist, depiction of priests breaking vows of chastity and accepting drug monies, a sexual encounter with fleeting nudity, an abortion, brief violence and intermittent rough language, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops classification is O -- morally offensive. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
